Summary

This project investigates whether a song’s audio features, genre, and release era can predict whether a Billboard Hot 100 song reaches the Top 10. Using historical Billboard chart data and Spotify audio features obtained from Kaggle, we developed a logistic regression classification model and compared its performance against a baseline model. Our tuned logistic regression model achieved an accuracy of 58.6%, recall of 65.0%, precision of 16.9%, and F1-score of 0.268 on the held-out test set. Although the model correctly identified approximately 65% of Top 10 songs, its low precision indicates that many songs predicted to reach the Top 10 did not actually do so. However, the baseline model achieved a higher accuracy of 88.3% but failed to identify any Top 10 songs. These findings suggest that audio features, genre, and release era provide limited predictive information about chart success. The imbalance between Top 10 and non-Top 10 songs, along with the model’s high number of false positives, are important limitations. Overall, the model is not yet reliable enough for predicting Top 10 chart success in practice.

Introduction

The Billboard Hot 100 is the main weekly ranking of the most popular songs in the United States. Songs are ranked using a combination of streaming, radio airplay and digital sales. Reaching the Top 10 of this chart is a major marker of commercial success. A Top 10 song typically brings an artist wider recognition, more radio play and greater visibility on streaming platforms.

Predicting which songs will become hits is valuable to many people in the music industry. If the way a song sounds can help predict its success, record labels and streaming services could make more informed decisions about where to invest their time and money. Additionally, this information could help new artists break into the music industry.

Spotify audio features, which describe characteristics of a song such as its danceability, energy and tempo, are widely used in music research, for example in predicting Spotify audio features from Last.fm tags (Castillo, Flores, and Leray 2024). Our research question is: can a song’s audio features, genre and release era predict whether it reaches the Top 10?

To answer this question, we use the “Billboard Hot Weekly Charts” dataset from Kaggle (The Devastator 2023) originally compiled by Sean Miller (Miller 2023). It combines the weekly Billboard Hot 100 charts since 1958 with audio features for each song from Spotify’s Web API, such as danceability, energy, valence (how positive a song sounds) and tempo, as well as each song’s genre. After cleaning, each row in our data represents one song, with 24,074 songs in total. Our target variable is whether a song reached the Top 10: a song is classified as “Top 10” if its peak position on the Hot 100 was 10 or lower (that is, it reached the Top 10 at least once), and “Not Top 10” otherwise. Because every song in the data has a known peak position along with its audio features and genre, this data allows us to directly test whether these characteristics can predict Top 10 success.

Methods

Data

We use the “Billboard Hot Weekly Charts” dataset on Kaggle (The Devastator 2023), which was originally compiled by Sean Miller (Miller 2023). It has two files:

  • Hot Stuff records each song’s position on the Billboard Hot 100 for every week since 1958.
  • Hot 100 Audio Features records Spotify audio features and genre for songs on the chart.

The download code below fetches both files with the kagglehub package and saves them to data/raw/. We join the files on song title and performer, keeping songs found in both. Each song is kept once, using the week it reached its peak position. We then drop unused columns and rows with missing values, and save the result to data/processed/.

After cleaning, each row is one song, and the data has 24,074 songs. The target is whether a song reached the Top 10: a song is “Top 10” if its peak position was 10 or lower, and “Not Top 10” otherwise. The predictors are:

  • audio features: danceability, energy, valence, loudness, tempo, acousticness, speechiness, instrumentalness, liveness and track duration;
  • release era: the year of the song’s peak week;
  • primary genre: the first genre listed for the song;
  • explicit content: whether the track is marked explicit.

Keep one genre per song

Each song can have several genres (for example, [‘dance pop’, ‘pop’, ‘post-teen pop’]). We keep only the first one as a single string.

def first_genre(val):
    # if the column is empty/null/none, it returns NaN
    if pd.isna(val):
        return np.nan
    # real list/tuple already
    if isinstance(val, (list, tuple)):
        return val[0] if len(val) else np.nan
    # try to parse string like "['dance pop','pop']" or '["dance pop","pop"]'
    s = str(val).strip()
    try:
        parsed = ast.literal_eval(s)
        if isinstance(parsed, (list, tuple)) and parsed:
            return parsed[0]
    except Exception:
        pass
    # if it's a comma-separated string, take the first part
    if "," in s:
        return s.split(",")[0].strip().strip("'").strip('"')
    # otherwise just return as-is
    return s

# keep original, write cleaned value to a new column
df_final["primary_genre"] = df_final["spotify_genre"].apply(first_genre)

Parameters
transformers transformers: list of tuples

List of (name, transformer, columns) tuples specifying the
transformer objects to be applied to subsets of the data.

name : str
Like in Pipeline and FeatureUnion, this allows the transformer and
its parameters to be set using ``set_params`` and searched in grid
search.
transformer : {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator
Estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.
Special-cased strings 'drop' and 'passthrough' are accepted as
well, to indicate to drop the columns or to pass them through
untransformed, respectively.
columns : str, array-like of str, int, array-like of int, array-like of bool, slice or callable
Indexes the data on its second axis. Integers are interpreted as
positional columns, while strings can reference DataFrame columns
by name. A scalar string or int should be used where
``transformer`` expects X to be a 1d array-like (vector),
otherwise a 2d array will be passed to the transformer.
A callable is passed the input data `X` and can return any of the
above. To select multiple columns by name or dtype, you can use
:obj:`make_column_selector`.		 [('pipeline-1', ...), ('pipeline-2', ...), ...]
remainder remainder: {'drop', 'passthrough'} or estimator, default='drop'

By default, only the specified columns in `transformers` are
transformed and combined in the output, and the non-specified
columns are dropped. (default of ``'drop'``).
By specifying ``remainder='passthrough'``, all remaining columns that
were not specified in `transformers`, but present in the data passed
to `fit` will be automatically passed through. This subset of columns
is concatenated with the output of the transformers. For dataframes,
extra columns not seen during `fit` will be excluded from the output
of `transform`.
By setting ``remainder`` to be an estimator, the remaining
non-specified columns will use the ``remainder`` estimator. The
estimator must support :term:`fit` and :term:`transform`.
Note that using this feature requires that the DataFrame columns
input at :term:`fit` and :term:`transform` have identical order.		 'drop'
sparse_threshold sparse_threshold: float, default=0.3

If the output of the different transformers contains sparse matrices,
these will be stacked as a sparse matrix if the overall density is
lower than this value. Use ``sparse_threshold=0`` to always return
dense. When the transformed output consists of all dense data, the
stacked result will be dense, and this keyword will be ignored.		 0.3
n_jobs n_jobs: int, default=None

Number of jobs to run in parallel.
``None`` means 1 unless in a :obj:`joblib.parallel_backend` context.
``-1`` means using all processors. See :term:`Glossary <n_jobs>`

Multiplicative weights for features per transformer. The output of the

verbose_feature_names_out verbose_feature_names_out: bool, str or Callable[[str, str], str], default=True

- If True, :meth:`ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out` will prefix

`verbose_feature_names_out="{transformer_name}__{feature_name}"`.
- If False, :meth:`ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out` will not
prefix any feature names and will error if feature names are not
unique.
- If ``Callable[[str, str], str]``,
:meth:`ColumnTransformer.get_feature_names_out` will rename all the features
using the name of the transformer. The first argument of the callable is the
transformer name and the second argument is the feature name. The returned
string will be the new feature name.
- If ``str``, it must be a string ready for formatting. The given string will
be formatted using two field names: ``transformer_name`` and ``feature_name``.
e.g. ``"{feature_name}__{transformer_name}"``. See :meth:`str.format` method
from the standard library for more info.

Parameters
strategy strategy: str or Callable, default='mean'

The imputation strategy.

- If "mean", then replace missing values using the mean along
each column. Can only be used with numeric data.
- If "median", then replace missing values using the median along
each column. Can only be used with numeric data.
- If "most_frequent", then replace missing using the most frequent
value along each column. Can be used with strings or numeric data.
If there is more than one such value, only the smallest is returned.
- If "constant", then replace missing values with fill_value. Can be
used with strings or numeric data.
- If an instance of Callable, then replace missing values using the
scalar statistic returned by running the callable over a dense 1d
array containing non-missing values of each column.

.. versionadded:: 0.20
strategy="constant" for fixed value imputation.

.. versionadded:: 1.5
strategy=callable for custom value imputation.		 'median'

The placeholder for the missing values. All occurrences of
`missing_values` will be imputed. For pandas' dataframes with
nullable integer dtypes with missing values, `missing_values`
can be set to either `np.nan` or `pd.NA`.		 nan
fill_value fill_value: str or numerical value, default=None

When strategy == "constant", `fill_value` is used to replace all
occurrences of missing_values. For string or object data types,
`fill_value` must be a string.
If `None`, `fill_value` will be 0 when imputing numerical
data and "missing_value" for strings or object data types.		 None
copy copy: bool, default=True

If True, a copy of X will be created. If False, imputation will
be done in-place whenever possible. Note that, in the following cases,
a new copy will always be made, even if `copy=False`:

- If `X` is not an array of floating values;
- If `X` is encoded as a CSR matrix;
- If `add_indicator=True`.		 True
add_indicator add_indicator: bool, default=False

If True, a :class:`MissingIndicator` transform will stack onto output
of the imputer's transform. This allows a predictive estimator
to account for missingness despite imputation. If a feature has no
missing values at fit/train time, the feature won't appear on
the missing indicator even if there are missing values at
transform/test time.		 False

If True, features that consist exclusively of missing values when

The imputed value is always `0` except when `strategy="constant"`
in which case `fill_value` will be used instead.

handle_unknown handle_unknown: {'error', 'ignore', 'infrequent_if_exist', 'warn'}, default='error'

Specifies the way unknown categories are handled during :meth:`transform`.

- 'error' : Raise an error if an unknown category is present during transform.
- 'ignore' : When an unknown category is encountered during
transform, the resulting one-hot encoded columns for this feature
will be all zeros. In the inverse transform, an unknown category
will be denoted as None.
- 'infrequent_if_exist' : When an unknown category is encountered
during transform, the resulting one-hot encoded columns for this
feature will map to the infrequent category if it exists. The
infrequent category will be mapped to the last position in the
encoding. During inverse transform, an unknown category will be
mapped to the category denoted `'infrequent'` if it exists. If the
`'infrequent'` category does not exist, then :meth:`transform` and
:meth:`inverse_transform` will handle an unknown category as with
`handle_unknown='ignore'`. Infrequent categories exist based on
`min_frequency` and `max_categories`. Read more in the
:ref:`User Guide <encoder_infrequent_categories>`.
- 'warn' : When an unknown category is encountered during transform
a warning is issued, and the encoding then proceeds as described for
`handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist"`.

.. versionchanged:: 1.1
`'infrequent_if_exist'` was added to automatically handle unknown
categories and infrequent categories.

.. versionadded:: 1.6
The option `"warn"` was added in 1.6.		 'ignore'
categories categories: 'auto' or a list of array-like, default='auto'

Categories (unique values) per feature:

- 'auto' : Determine categories automatically from the training data.
- list : ``categories[i]`` holds the categories expected in the ith
column. The passed categories should not mix strings and numeric
values within a single feature, and should be sorted in case of
numeric values.

The used categories can be found in the ``categories_`` attribute.

.. versionadded:: 0.20		 'auto'
drop drop: {'first', 'if_binary'} or an array-like of shape (n_features,), default=None

Specifies a methodology to use to drop one of the categories per
feature. This is useful in situations where perfectly collinear
features cause problems, such as when feeding the resulting data
into an unregularized linear regression model.

However, dropping one category breaks the symmetry of the original
representation and can therefore induce a bias in downstream models,
for instance for penalized linear classification or regression models.

- None : retain all features (the default).
- 'first' : drop the first category in each feature. If only one
category is present, the feature will be dropped entirely.
- 'if_binary' : drop the first category in each feature with two
categories. Features with 1 or more than 2 categories are
left intact.
- array : ``drop[i]`` is the category in feature ``X[:, i]`` that
should be dropped.

When `max_categories` or `min_frequency` is configured to group
infrequent categories, the dropping behavior is handled after the
grouping.

.. versionadded:: 0.21
The parameter `drop` was added in 0.21.

.. versionchanged:: 0.23
The option `drop='if_binary'` was added in 0.23.

- None : retain all features (the default).
- 'first' : drop the first category in each feature. If only one
category is present, the feature will be dropped entirely.
- 'if_binary' : drop the first category in each feature with two
categories. Features with 1 or more than 2 categories are
left intact.
- array : ``drop[i]`` is the category in feature ``X[:, i]`` that
should be dropped.

When `max_categories` or `min_frequency` is configured to group
infrequent categories, the dropping behavior is handled after the
grouping.

.. versionadded:: 0.21
The parameter `drop` was added in 0.21.

.. versionchanged:: 0.23
The option `drop='if_binary'` was added in 0.23.

.. versionchanged:: 1.1
Support for dropping infrequent categories.		 'if_binary'
sparse_output sparse_output: bool, default=True

When ``True``, it returns a SciPy sparse matrix/array
in "Compressed Sparse Row" (CSR) format.

.. versionadded:: 1.2
`sparse` was renamed to `sparse_output`		 False
categories categories: 'auto' or a list of array-like, default='auto'

Categories (unique values) per feature:

- 'auto' : Determine categories automatically from the training data.
- list : ``categories[i]`` holds the categories expected in the ith
column. The passed categories should not mix strings and numeric
values within a single feature, and should be sorted in case of
numeric values.

The used categories can be found in the ``categories_`` attribute.

.. versionadded:: 0.20		 'auto'
dtype dtype: number type, default=np.float64

Desired dtype of output.		 <class 'numpy.float64'>
handle_unknown handle_unknown: {'error', 'ignore', 'infrequent_if_exist', 'warn'}, default='error'

Specifies the way unknown categories are handled during :meth:`transform`.

- 'error' : Raise an error if an unknown category is present during transform.
- 'ignore' : When an unknown category is encountered during
transform, the resulting one-hot encoded columns for this feature
will be all zeros. In the inverse transform, an unknown category
will be denoted as None.
- 'infrequent_if_exist' : When an unknown category is encountered
during transform, the resulting one-hot encoded columns for this
feature will map to the infrequent category if it exists. The
infrequent category will be mapped to the last position in the
encoding. During inverse transform, an unknown category will be
mapped to the category denoted `'infrequent'` if it exists. If the
`'infrequent'` category does not exist, then :meth:`transform` and
:meth:`inverse_transform` will handle an unknown category as with
`handle_unknown='ignore'`. Infrequent categories exist based on
`min_frequency` and `max_categories`. Read more in the
:ref:`User Guide <encoder_infrequent_categories>`.
- 'warn' : When an unknown category is encountered during transform
a warning is issued, and the encoding then proceeds as described for
`handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist"`.

.. versionchanged:: 1.1
`'infrequent_if_exist'` was added to automatically handle unknown
categories and infrequent categories.

.. versionadded:: 1.6
The option `"warn"` was added in 1.6.		 'error'
min_frequency min_frequency: int or float, default=None

Specifies the minimum frequency below which a category will be
considered infrequent.

- If `int`, categories with a smaller cardinality will be considered
infrequent.

- If `float`, categories with a smaller cardinality than
`min_frequency * n_samples` will be considered infrequent.

.. versionadded:: 1.1
Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <encoder_infrequent_categories>`.		 None
max_categories max_categories: int, default=None

Specifies an upper limit to the number of output features for each input
feature when considering infrequent categories. If there are infrequent
categories, `max_categories` includes the category representing the
infrequent categories along with the frequent categories. If `None`,
there is no limit to the number of output features.

.. versionadded:: 1.1
Read more in the :ref:`User Guide <encoder_infrequent_categories>`.		 None
feature_name_combiner feature_name_combiner: "concat" or callable, default="concat"

Callable with signature `def callable(input_feature, category)` that returns a
string. This is used to create feature names to be returned by
:meth:`get_feature_names_out`.

`"concat"` concatenates encoded feature name and category with
`feature + "_" + str(category)`.E.g. feature X with values 1, 6, 7 create
feature names `X_1, X_6, X_7`.

.. versionadded:: 1.3		 'concat'

Baseline model

dummy_pipe = make_pipeline(preprocessor, DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent"))

scoring = ["accuracy", "precision", "recall", "f1"]
cv_dummy = cross_validate(dummy_pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=5,
                          scoring=scoring, return_train_score=True)

results = {"Dummy (most frequent)": pd.DataFrame(cv_dummy).mean()}

Logistic regression

lr_pipe = make_pipeline(preprocessor, LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=522))

param_grid = {
    "logisticregression__C": np.logspace(-3, 3, 7),
    "logisticregression__class_weight": [None, "balanced"],
}

search = GridSearchCV(
    lr_pipe, param_grid, cv=5,
    scoring=scoring, refit="f1",
    return_train_score=True, n_jobs=1,
)
search.fit(X_train, y_train)
search.best_params_
{'logisticregression__C': np.float64(0.1),
 'logisticregression__class_weight': 'balanced'}
best = pd.DataFrame(search.cv_results_).iloc[search.best_index_]
results["Logistic regression (tuned)"] = pd.Series({
    f"{split}_{m}": best[f"mean_{split}_{m}"]
    for split in ["train", "test"] for m in scoring
})

table2 = (
    pd.DataFrame(results).T
    .loc[["Dummy (most frequent)", "Logistic regression (tuned)"],
         ["test_accuracy", "test_precision", "test_recall", "test_f1"]]
    .round(3)
)
table2.columns = ["Accuracy", "Precision", "Recall", "F1"]
table2

Modelling Methods

In our analysis, we chose to compare a baseline dummy model to a logistic regression model. Our dummy model learns the most common target class within our data and always predicts that class (Not Top 10), which represents a model that does not learn any useful statistical patterns from the data. The main model we chose for this analysis is the logistic regression model, which predicts either a positive (Top 10) or negative (Not Top 10) class using learned patterns from the data.

We tuned the logistic regression using a grid search with 5-fold cross-validation, trying different values of the regularization strength C (0.001 to 1,000) and either no class weighting or balanced class weights. Since only about 12% of songs reached the Top 10, we chose the model with the best F1 score instead of the best accuracy.

Results & Discussion

Exploratory data analysis

# Table 2: average audio feature values for Top 10 vs. non-Top 10 songs
# (training data only)
table_1 = (
    train_df
    .groupby("top_10")[["danceability", "energy", "valence", "loudness", "tempo"]]
    .mean()
    .round(2)
)

# add number of songs in each group
table_1.insert(0, "Number of songs", train_df["top_10"].value_counts().sort_index())

# readable labels
table_1.index = ["Not Top 10", "Top 10"]
table_1.columns = ["Number of songs", "Danceability", "Energy", "Valence",
                   "Loudness (dB)", "Tempo (BPM)"]
table_1
Number of songs Danceability Energy Valence Loudness (dB) Tempo (BPM)
Not Top 10 14770 0.60 0.62 0.60 -8.64 120.30
Top 10 2081 0.62 0.62 0.63 -8.69 119.48

Table 2: Summary of audio features by Top 10 status.

Table 2 summarizes the average values of five audio features for songs that did and did not reach the Top 10 in the training data. We selected these five features (danceability, energy, valence, loudness and tempo) because they are commonly used to describe a song’s overall sound. The differences between the two groups are quite small. Top 10 songs are slightly more danceable (0.62 vs. 0.60) and have slightly higher valence (0.63 vs. 0.60), while energy, loudness and tempo are nearly identical. This tells us that no single audio feature strongly separates Top 10 songs from other songs.

# Figure 1: number of songs that did and did not reach the Top 10
# (training data only)
class_counts = (
    train_df["top_10"]
    .map({0: "Not Top 10", 1: "Top 10"})
    .value_counts()
    .reset_index()
)
class_counts.columns = ["Top 10 status", "Number of songs"]

alt.Chart(class_counts).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X("Top 10 status", title="Top 10 status", axis=alt.Axis(labelAngle=0)),
    y=alt.Y("Number of songs", title="Number of songs"),
    color=alt.Color("Top 10 status", legend=None)
).properties(
    width=300,
    height=300,
    title="Number of songs by Top 10 status (training data)"
).configure_axis(
    labelFontSize=13,
    titleFontSize=14
).configure_title(
    fontSize=16
).configure_legend(
    labelFontSize=13,
    titleFontSize=14
)

Figure 1: Class balance of Top 10 vs. non-Top 10 songs.

Figure 1 shows the number of songs in each class. We used a bar chart because it makes it easy to compare the counts of the two categories. The classes are highly imbalanced: only 2,081 songs (about 12%) reached the Top 10, compared to 14,770 songs that did not. Due to the imbalance, using only accuracy would be misleading (He and Garcia 2009), since a model that always predicted “Not Top 10” would still be about 88% accurate. Instead, we should use metrics such as recall and F1 score, which better reflect how well the model identifies Top 10 songs.

# Figure 2: distribution of danceability by Top 10 status
# (training data only)
plot_df = train_df.assign(
    top_10_label=train_df["top_10"].map({0: "Not Top 10", 1: "Top 10"})
)[["danceability", "top_10_label"]]

alt.Chart(plot_df).transform_density(
    "danceability",
    groupby=["top_10_label"],
    as_=["danceability", "density"]
).mark_area(opacity=0.5).encode(
    x=alt.X("danceability:Q", title="Danceability (0 = least, 1 = most danceable)"),
    y=alt.Y("density:Q", title="Density", stack=None),
    color=alt.Color("top_10_label:N", title="Top 10 status")
).properties(
    width=400,
    height=300,
    title="Distribution of danceability by Top 10 status (training data)"
).configure_axis(
    labelFontSize=13,
    titleFontSize=14
).configure_title(
    fontSize=16
).configure_legend(
    labelFontSize=13,
    titleFontSize=14
)

Figure 2: Danceability of Top 10 vs. non-Top 10 songs.

Figure 2 shows the distribution of danceability for Top 10 and non-Top 10 songs. The Top 10 distribution is shifted slightly to the right, meaning Top 10 songs tend to be a little more danceable. However, the significant overlap suggests that danceability is not enough to predict Top 10 status. This is consistent with the small differences seen in Table 2.

Overall, the EDA suggests that no single audio feature strongly distinguishes Top 10 songs from other songs. Therefore, we should use all the audio features (danceability, energy, valence, loudness, tempo, acousticness, speechiness, instrumentalness, liveness, duration and explicit content) while including the other features primary genre and era as well. We shouldn’t include peak position, week position, weeks on chart or Spotify popularity because these features give the model information about the target. This would make the model look more accurate than it really is, since it would not have this information when predicting a new song.

Test set evaluation

dummy_pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)

models = {
    "Dummy (most frequent)": dummy_pipe,
    "Logistic regression (tuned)": search.best_estimator_,
}

rows = {}
for name, model in models.items():
    y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
    rows[name] = {
        "Accuracy":  accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred),
        "Precision": precision_score(y_test, y_pred, zero_division=0),
        "Recall":    recall_score(y_test, y_pred),
        "F1":        f1_score(y_test, y_pred),
    }

table3 = pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3)

Modelling Results

Table 1 shows the cross-validation results. The baseline has a high accuracy (0.877) but an F1 score of 0, because it never predicts a Top 10 song. The tuned logistic regression (C = 0.1, balanced class weights) reached an F1 score of 0.277. It found about 65% of Top 10 songs (recall of 0.648), but only about 18% of its predicted hits were correct (precision of 0.176).

On the test set (Table 3), the tuned logistic regression reached an F1 score of 0.268, with a recall of 0.65 and a precision of 0.169. These scores are very close to the cross-validation scores in Table 1 (F1 of 0.277), which suggests the cross-validation results were a reliable estimate of how the model performs on new songs. The confusion matrix in Figure 3 shows the same pattern: the model correctly identifies most of the songs that reached the Top 10, but it also predicts many songs as hits that did not make it, which is why its precision is low.

Overall, the model does better than the baseline, but the audio features, genre and era only give a weak signal for predicting Top 10 hits.

The text above was drafted with help from Claude. Anthropic. (2026). Claude (Opus 5.5 version) [Large language model]. https://claude.ai

Discussion

Our results suggest that a song’s audio features, genre and release era can predict whether it reaches the Top 10 only to a limited extent. The tuned logistic regression identified about two thirds of Top 10 songs on the test set, but most songs it predicted as hits did not actually reach the Top 10 so it would not be reliable enough for record labels or streaming services to base investment decisions on. However, these findings are in line with our exploratory data analysis, which showed only small differences in audio features between Top 10 and non-Top 10 songs.

Based on these results, future models could include additional information that is not captured by a song’s sound, such as marketing and promotion data and the artist’s existing popularity (for example, their previous chart success). Future work could also test whether models that capture interactions between features, such as a random forest, lead to better predictions.
